topic: Electrical solver class for the MINIVAC 601 simulator core: boolean connectivity vs DC resistive network, and the named parameter profile it runs on
agent_note: This gap is NOT closable from the published record. I confirmed by exhaustive read that Scientific Development Corporation published exactly five electrical numbers about the machine (110 V AC in, 12 V DC nominal out, ~13 V unloaded out, 1.5 A continuous, and switch/contact current ratings) and deliberately published ZERO relay or lamp parameters. Book VII prints a blank table and orders the owner to measure. Therefore this file does two things: (1) it makes the SOLVER CLASS ruling, which the sources DO settle decisively; (2) it proposes a NAMED FALLBACK parameter profile, MV601-REF-A, derived by constraint satisfaction against the behaviours SDC did document, together with a fidelity contract of executable acceptance tests. The profile numbers are inference and are tagged [unverified] individually; what is [verified] is the set of behaviours they are required to reproduce. I also correct a prior finding: the lamp-resistance figure proposed in find-relays.json (~40 ohm at the series operating point) is too LOW and, if used, silently erases the only relay failure SDC ever documented. See CORRECTION-01.

part_1_the_complete_published_electrical.note: This is the exhaustive set. I grepped all six books plus errata plus maintenance manual for every occurrence of ohm, volt, amp, milliamp, watt, current, resistance. Nothing else exists.

claims.claim: Mains input is 110 volts AC. The power supply converts it to a low DC level of 12 volts.
claims.citation: BK1 OCR lines 107-109 and 149; MM p.3 step 4 ('Check the 110 volt outlet')
claims.quote: the power supply converts the 110-volt AC power obtained ... level of 12 volts DC. This low voltage DC is used to ...

claims.claim: The power supply is rated at 1.5 amps continuous with a nominal 12 volts output.
claims.citation: MM printed p.2, section 'Adjustment and Repair'
claims.quote: The power supply is rated at 1.5 amps continuous with a nominal 12 volts output.

claims.claim: The UNLOADED power supply outlet voltage should be approximately 13 volts.
claims.citation: MM printed p.3, troubleshooting step 3 (read from page image pages/maintenance/p-05.png)
claims.quote: The unloaded power supply outlet voltage should be approximately 13 volts.

claims.claim: All switches are rated at 3 amps; relay contacts are rated in excess of 3 amps.
claims.citation: MM printed p.2
claims.quote: All switches are rated at 3 amps; relay contacts are rated in excess of 3 amps.

claims.claim: The lights are operated at LESS than their rated voltage to extend their operating life. They are described again later as 'conservatively operated' and expected to last at least a year.
claims.citation: MM printed p.2 and printed p.6 ('Lights')
claims.quote: The lights are operated at less than their rated voltage to extend their operating life.

claims.claim: The drive motor is operated at less than one-third rated voltage.
claims.citation: MM printed p.2
claims.quote: The drive motor is operated at less than one-third rated voltage.

claims.claim: Book VII's resistor colour-code worked example is a RED-RED-BLACK-GOLD resistor = 22 ohms +/-5%. This is the only resistor value printed in the entire Book VII tutorial text.
claims.citation: BK7 printed p.6 (PDF p.11), read from page image
claims.quote: RED-RED represents 22 / BLACK represents no '0' / GOLD represents +/-5% ... This resistor has a resistance of: 22 ohms +/-5%

claims.claim: A Book VII footnote names 15, 22 or 33 ohms as resistors used to SLOW THE MOTOR. These are motor-circuit values, not relay bias values, and must not be confused with the bias resistor set.
claims.citation: BK7 OCR, footnote to the automatic counter program
claims.quote: This is an optional connection. Use a 15, 22 or 33 ohm resistor to decrease the speed of the motor.

claims.claim: The rotary-switch motor drive contains TWO current-limiting resistors whose stated function is explicitly analogised to the indicator lamps: SDC says the resistors limit current 'in the same way that the lights limit the amount of current which flows through a relay coil'. Their values are never given. A maintenance test says they should heat up in about 20 seconds with power across them.
claims.citation: MM printed p.10, step 3; and the rotary-switch motor drive text quoted in find-relays.json
claims.significance: SDC itself classifies the series indicator lamp as a deliberate CURRENT-LIMITING RESISTOR. This is the strongest published statement about the lamp's electrical role.

claims.claim: The published power supply schematic contains NO FILTER CAPACITOR. Topology, read directly off the diagram: power cord -> POWER SWITCH in one primary leg -> TRANSFORMER primary; centre-tapped secondary -> two yellow/black end leads feed the two diodes of a RECTIFIER whose common output is the + terminal; the yellow centre-tap lead passes through the CIRCUIT BREAKER to the - terminal; the POWER LIGHT sits across + and -. Nothing else is drawn.
claims.citation: MM printed p.3, 'Power Supply Circuit Diagram', read from page image pages/maintenance/p-05.png
claims.significance: The rails carry unfiltered full-wave-rectified 120 Hz pulsating DC. See EL-11 and OQ-03.

claims.claim: Because there is no filter capacitor (EL-10), the '13 volts unloaded' of EL-03 is an AVERAGE value as read by a 1961 average-responding DC voltmeter. The instantaneous peak of a full-wave rectified sine at 13 V average is about 20.4 V (V_peak = V_avg * pi/2).
claims.citation: inference from EL-03 + EL-10
claims.why_likely_not_verified: SDC does not state what instrument or what quantity. The reading could also have been taken on a meter with a different response. But an unfiltered full-wave supply plus an average-reading DC meter is by far the most probable 1961 combination.

claims.claim: The circuit breaker is in the NEGATIVE return (the transformer centre-tap line), so it sees TOTAL machine current, not per-branch current. SDC expects programming errors to trip it.
claims.citation: MM printed p.3 diagram; ERR p.1 ('If a programming error has caused a short circuit, push the circuit breaker after correcting the error.')

claims.claim: All + terminals are one node and all - terminals are one node, including M+ and M-.
claims.citation: ERR p.1
claims.quote: All + and - terminals are connected together. For example, a connection to 1+ is the same as a connection to 3+, 6+, or M+. Similarly, a connection to 2- is the same as a connection to 4-, 5-, or M-.

claims.claim: NOTHING ELSE IS PUBLISHED. Books I through VI contain no electrical figure at all beyond '110-volt AC' and '12 volts DC'. There is no coil resistance, no lamp resistance, no lamp part number or bulb type, no pull-in voltage, no drop-out voltage, no source impedance, and no list of the resistor values supplied in the Book VII kit, anywhere in the corpus.
claims.citation: exhaustive grep of book1.txt, book2-3-4.txt, book5-6.txt for ohm|volt|amp|milliamp|watt|current|resistance; plus full read of MM, ERR and BK7
claims.method_note: The only hits in Books I-VI were BK1:107-112 and BK1:149 (110 V AC / 12 V DC), plus two unrelated hits in Book III's analogue-computer discussion about 'amps of current as analogues of pounds of salt'.

part_2_the_behaviours_that_force_the_rul.note: These are the documented behaviours that a boolean connectivity core provably cannot represent. Each is verified from a primary page.

claims.claim: SERIES LAMP TOPOLOGY. Three terminals sit above each relay: C, E, F. The indicator lamp is hard-wired between C and E; the coil is hard-wired between E and F; E is the shared midpoint. Driving C-to-F puts lamp AND coil in series. Driving E-to-F drives the coil alone at full rail. Driving C-to-E lights the lamp with no coil current.
claims.citation: BK1 printed p.14 schematic 'C -- [LIGHT] -- E -- [RELAY COIL] -- F', panel legend brackets LIGHT over C-E and COIL over E-F; independently re-confirmed by me in the ERR alternate-counter diagram where each relay is drawn as 'nC -(lamp)- nE -(coil)- nF'
claims.prior_work: established in find-relays.json; I re-verified it independently on the errata diagram

claims.claim: SDC EXPLICITLY DOCUMENTS A VOLTAGE FAILURE. The errata note for Book IV p.72 says the three-bit binary counter strains the relays, that relays which work everywhere else may fail in this circuit, and that the fix is a circuit that bypasses the indicator lights so that FULL VOLTAGE reaches the coils and they pull in MORE RELIABLY.
claims.citation: ERR p.2, BOOK IV, page 72 note, read from page image at 200 dpi
claims.quote: Note on 'Three-Bit Binary Counter' - the design of this counter is such that the capabilities of the relays are somewhat strained. Relays which perform to satisfaction in every other case may not perform adequately in this circuit. If the counter in Book IV does not perform correctly, use the program and circuit which follow. The circuit below by-passes the relay indicator lights so that full voltage is supplied to the relay coils, causing them to pull in more reliably.
claims.significance: This is the single most important sentence in the corpus for this gap. Two circuits with IDENTICAL boolean connectivity semantics (coil energised / coil not energised) have DIFFERENT observable outcomes. A boolean core makes both succeed and therefore cannot express the only relay failure SDC ever published.

claims.claim: THE BYPASS IS A SERIES-TO-SHUNT MOVE, NOT A DISCONNECTION. In the alternate counter the lamp is still present and still lights; the program ties each relay's C terminal to the negative rail (2C/2-, 4C/4-, 6C/6-, chained via 1C/2C, 3C/4C, 5C/6C), so the lamp hangs from E to - as a SHUNT while the drive current runs through the coil between E and F. Coil terminals E and F carry the logic (1A/2E, 1E/2G, 2E/2J, 1F/2F, 1F/1H, 3F/3H, 3F/4F, 4E/4J, 5F/6F, 5F/5H, 6E/6J).
claims.citation: ERR p.2, alternate counter circuit diagram and its 48-connection program list, read from page image at 200 dpi
claims.significance: KILLER ARGUMENT against a cheap heuristic. A boolean core patched with a rule like 'a coil driven through a lamp is marginal' still gets this wrong: here the lamp IS electrically attached to the coil node, but as a shunt. Only an actual network solve distinguishes series from shunt. Any topological path analysis capable of making that distinction has already done most of the work of the solve.

claims.claim: THE CANONICAL LATCH DRIVES THROUGH THE LAMP ON BOTH PATHS. Book I Experiment 9's two-pushbutton relay memory sets via 2+ -> 2Y -> 1Y -> 1X -> 1C -> LAMP -> 1E -> COIL -> 1F -> 1-, and holds via 2+ -> 2Y -> 2Z -> 1L -> 1K -> 1C -> LAMP -> COIL -> 1F -> 1-. The coil therefore NEVER sees rail voltage in the simplest published relay circuit, yet it must both pull in and hold.
claims.citation: BK1 Experiment 9, program and text; transcribed in find-relays.json and consistent with BH-01
claims.significance: This is the lower bound. It pins pull-in BELOW the lamp-divided voltage. BH-02 pins it ABOVE the lamp-divided voltage under load. Together they bracket the answer, which is why the profile in Part 4 is constrained at all rather than free.

claims.claim: BOOK I TEACHES THE C-vs-E DISTINCTION DIRECTLY. Experiment 7 drives the coil via 1X/1E and then instructs the reader to REMOVE 1X/1E and ADD 1X/1C to make the indicator lamp light. SDC's own text says that if the coil is energised through E and F the light will NOT come on 'because there is no current flowing through the light'.
claims.citation: BK1 Experiment 7 step 6 and BK1 printed p.14 body text
claims.significance: The manual itself treats C-drive and E-drive as electrically different operations from the very first relay lesson.

claims.claim: BOOK VII IS BUILT ENTIRELY ON THE HYSTERESIS BAND. It defines pull-in and drop-out voltages, states that MINIVAC relays are DELIBERATELY designed for a large gap between them, and shows a graph of a bi-stable shaded region between drop-out and pull-in, with a bias voltage placed inside it. The whole technique is: hold the coil inside the band with a series resistor so the relay latches without consuming a contact.
claims.citation: BK7 printed pp.6-7 (PDF pp.11-12), read from page images
claims.quote: The voltage at which a relay turns on is called the 'pull-in' voltage; the voltage at which a relay turns off is called the 'drop-out' voltage. The MINIVAC's relays are deliberately designed so that there is a great difference between the 'pull-in' and 'drop-out' voltages.
claims.quote2: By placing an appropriate resistor between power and the relay coil, we can insure that the voltage supplied to the relay will fall within the region defined by the 'pull-in' and 'drop-out' voltages. Then, if we constantly supply power to the relay coil, the relay will be a bi-stable element and both sets of contacts will be free.

claims.claim: THE BOOK VII HYSTERESIS GRAPHS CARRY NO NUMBERS. Both graphs on printed p.7 are drawn with unlabelled axes. The x-axis is annotated only 'DROP-OUT VOLTAGE', 'BIAS VOLTAGE', 'PULL-IN VOLTAGE', 'VOLTAGE -> (TO FULL POWER SUPPLY VOLTAGE)'. The y-axis is annotated only 'RELAY ON' and 'RELAY OFF'. There are no tick values anywhere.
claims.citation: BK7 printed p.7 (PDF p.12), read from page image
claims.significance: SDC's refusal to publish numbers is deliberate and total, not an omission I failed to find. The ONE thing the graph does fix is the ORDERING: 0 < drop-out < bias < pull-in < full supply voltage.

claims.claim: THE BIAS TABLE IS PRINTED BLANK AND THE OWNER IS ORDERED TO MEASURE. Book VII printed p.9 shows a two-column chart, relay 1-6 against 'value of bias resistance (in ohms)', with the six entries printed as Omega-B1 = , Omega-B2 = , Omega-B3 = , Omega-B4 = , Omega-B5 = , Omega-B6 = and nothing after the equals signs. Printed p.8 states in capitals: 'THE FOLLOWING INSTRUCTIONS ARE FOR A SINGLE RELAY. THIS PROCEDURE MUST BE CARRIED OUT FOR EACH INDIVIDUAL RELAY.'
claims.citation: BK7 printed pp.8-9 (PDF pp.13-14), read from page images
claims.significance: SDC is telling the owner that the six relays in one machine differ enough to need individual characterisation. Per-relay parameter spread is therefore a VERIFIED design property of the real machine, not a simulator affectation.

claims.claim: THE BIAS PROCEDURE IS A DESCENDING SEARCH BOUNDED BY THE KIT. Wire + -> RESISTOR -> E -> RELAY COIL -> F -> -, with pushbutton contact X on E and pushbutton arm Y on +, so pressing the button shorts the bias resistor and slams full rail onto E. Program: A/G, B/-, E/X, F/-, H/+, Y/+, (+/Omega, Omega/E). The footnote says: 'Decreasing values of resistance will be tried here. Start with the highest valued resistor in the kit.' Step 1: power on, relay must remain OFF. Step 2: press and release the button, relay must remain ON. The bias resistor is the LOWEST resistance passing both.
claims.citation: BK7 printed pp.8-9 (PDF pp.13-14), circuit diagram, program list and numbered procedure, read from page images
claims.significance_a: Note the bias current enters at E. The bias circuit BYPASSES the indicator lamp. So Book VII's band is measured on the bare coil, not on the lamp-plus-coil series pair.
claims.significance_b: 'the highest valued resistor in the kit' proves a graded set of discrete resistors shipped with Book VII, and constrains it: the top value must divide the rail below pull-in, and there must be a value low enough that the relay pulls in at power-on (otherwise the descent never terminates).

claims.claim: SDC ANTICIPATES MULTIPLE VALID BIAS VALUES PER RELAY.
claims.citation: BK7 printed p.9
claims.quote: You may find that more than one value of resistance will meet the requirements of the bias resistor for a relay. In this case, record both in the preceding chart. When using that relay's bias resistor in a program, try the lower valued resistor first; if the program does not operate properly, substitute the higher valued bias resistor for the relay.
claims.significance: The band is wide enough to admit several adjacent E12 values. Any candidate profile must reproduce that, not just admit one value.

claims.claim: A SECOND DOCUMENTED MARGINALITY. The errata for Book V p.11 Experiment 9 (the elevator) says: 'If the performance of the circuit is unsatisfactory, make the following changes to the program: remove 5F/6C, 6C/6-; add 5F/6E, 6E/6-, 4E/6C.' The change moves connections off C terminals onto E terminals.
claims.citation: ERR p.3, BOOK V page 11 note
claims.significance: A SECOND independent SDC fix of the same shape as BH-02: move the drive from C to E to get the lamp out of the coil's series path. Two independent occurrences make the phenomenon systemic, not a one-off. NOTE: this is Book V's Experiment 9, a different circuit from Book I's Experiment 9 in BH-04; do not conflate them.

claims.claim: SDC TREATS SPEED AND SETTLING AS REAL. The errata instructs users to push pushbutton 6 SLOWLY on the single-input flip-flop (Book IV p.69), to hold pushbutton 6 down long enough for carry to propagate to the highest stage of the alternate counter, and warns that 'some programs are not designed for high-speed operation'.
claims.citation: ERR p.1 (step 2 of the troubleshooting list) and ERR p.2 (Book IV p.69 note and the alternate counter Procedure)
claims.significance: Relay actuation time is observable and load-bearing. It is a separate axis from the voltage question but it lands in the same solver.

part_3_the_ruling.decision: The core is a DC RESISTIVE-NETWORK SOLVER, not a boolean connectivity solver.
part_3_the_ruling.one_line: Boolean connectivity is not merely less faithful here; it is incapable of expressing behaviours SDC published as errata, and adopting it would silently delete the only relay failure mode the manufacturer ever documented.
argument: BH-02 and BH-03 are decisive on their own. Two circuits identical under boolean connectivity semantics (the Book IV counter and its errata replacement) have different documented outcomes. Under a boolean core both succeed, so the errata becomes unrepresentable and the machine becomes MORE reliable than the real one.

BH-03 additionally defeats the obvious cheap patch. A rule of the form 'a coil driven through N lamps is degraded' fails on the alternate counter, where the lamp is attached to the coil node as a SHUNT and must NOT degrade anything. Series versus shunt is exactly what a network solve computes and what a connectivity walk does not.
BH-06, BH-08, BH-09 and BH-10 make an entire published book inexpressible without a continuous coil voltage and a two-threshold state rule.
EL-12 makes the circuit breaker a function of TOTAL current, which requires currents, which requires a solve.
EL-09 is SDC in its own words classifying the indicator lamp as a current-limiting resistor in the coil circuit.

The cost objection does not survive contact with the problem size. The network is tiny: on the order of 60 nodes and 30 two-terminal elements. A dense LU factorisation of a 60x60 matrix is microseconds. This is not a SPICE-scale problem and does not need a SPICE-scale engine.

rejected_alternatives.name: PROFILE-ZERO, pure boolean connectivity
rejected_alternatives.rejected_because: Cannot express BH-02, BH-06, BH-09, EL-12. Deletes the documented counter failure and makes Book VII impossible. Rejected outright.

rejected_alternatives.name: PROFILE-ZERO-PLUS, boolean plus a lamp-count-in-path heuristic
rejected_alternatives.rejected_because: Defeated by BH-03: it cannot distinguish the alternate counter's shunt lamp from a series lamp without path analysis that already amounts to a solve. Also still cannot express Book VII's bias band, the breaker, or two lamps in series. Rejected.

rejected_alternatives.name: Full transient SPICE with inductance on every coil
rejected_alternatives.rejected_because: Unnecessary for Books I-VI, which contain no reactive component. Reserve transient integration for Book VII capacitors only, behind a flag. Deferred, not rejected on principle.

what_a_net_means.ruling: A net is a NODE IN A CONDUCTANCE GRAPH, not a boolean equipotential class.
what_a_net_means.construction: Union-find over (a) patch wires and (b) currently-closed switch contacts, treating both as zero-ohm (or near-zero-ohm) shorts, yields the node set. Two-terminal ELEMENTS - relay coils, indicator lamps, user resistors, user capacitors, the motor and its two series resistors, and the source itself - span two nodes each and are NEVER collapsed by the union-find. So jack 1C and jack 1E are always distinct nodes even though the lamp joins them; jack 1+ and jack 3+ are always the same node (EL-13).
what_a_net_means.consequence: The solver returns a VOLTAGE per node and a CURRENT per element. Downstream logic (does relay n pull in, does lamp n glow and how brightly, does the breaker trip) reads those, and never reads connectivity directly.

part_4_named_fallback_profile.status: NAMED FALLBACK. This is a documented engineering decision, not a research result. Every number in it is inference and is tagged [unverified] individually. What is NOT inference is the constraint set in part_5 that these numbers were chosen to satisfy.
part_4_named_fallback_profile.derivation_method: Constraint satisfaction, not datasheet lookup. I treated the four documented behaviours (BH-02, BH-04, BH-09, EL-02) as simultaneous inequalities on the unknowns and searched for a consistent assignment. The search is tightly bounded: BH-04 requires the lamp-divided coil voltage to EXCEED pull-in on a lightly loaded machine, while BH-02 requires that same lamp-divided voltage to FALL BELOW pull-in for some relays on a fully loaded machine. Those two bracket pull-in to within a few tenths of a volt once the divider ratio is fixed.

parameters.name: supply_open_circuit_volts
parameters.provenance: EL-03, stated outright by MM p.3. The only rail number SDC gives that is not a rating.

parameters.name: supply_source_resistance_ohm
parameters.provenance: INFERENCE from EL-02 + EL-03: the rail falls from 13.0 V unloaded to 12.0 V 'nominal' at the 1.5 A continuous rating, so R = (13.0 - 12.0)/1.5 = 0.667 ohm. This reads 'nominal 12 volts output' as the loaded figure at rated current, which is the conventional way to state a supply rating but is NOT stated by SDC.
parameters.why_it_matters: Non-zero source impedance is what makes loads interact. With R_src = 0 the machine cannot exhibit BH-02 at all, because a lightly loaded and a heavily loaded machine become identical. Do not set this to zero.

parameters.name: relay_coil_resistance_ohm
parameters.provenance: CHOSEN. Fixed by the current budget, not by evidence: it must let six coils plus the lamp complement sit under the 1.5 A of EL-02 with the headroom implied by 'conservatively designed'. See AT-05.
parameters.why_weakly_constrained: The absolute value is the LEAST load-bearing number in the profile. See part_6 invariants: what matters is the RATIO R_coil/(R_coil+R_lamp) and the current budget, not the ohms themselves.

parameters.name: indicator_lamp_resistance_model
parameters.value: R(I) = clamp(R_cold, 2*R_hot, R_hot * (I/I_hot)^0.36) with R_hot = 160 ohm at I_hot = 81 mA, R_cold = 18 ohm
parameters.provenance: CHOSEN, tungsten-filament power law. Anchored so that a lamp alone across the rail draws ~81 mA at ~160 ohm (a lamp in the 12-14 V, sub-100 mA class, consistent with EL-05's 'operated at less than their rated voltage'), and so that the same lamp in series with a coil runs cooler at ~46 mA and ~131 ohm.
parameters.why_it_matters: THIS IS THE MOST IMPORTANT NUMBER IN THE PROFILE and the one a naive build gets wrong. See CORRECTION-01.

parameters.name: relay_pull_in_volts_nominal
parameters.provenance: CHOSEN, but tightly bracketed by BH-04 (must be below 6.93 V, the lightly loaded lamp-divided coil voltage, or the canonical latch fails) and BH-02 (must be near or above 6.67 V for at least some relays under full load, or the counter failure vanishes). The usable window is roughly 6.2 to 6.9 V.
parameters.per_relay_spread: +/- 0.7 V, seeded per relay instance and stable for the life of the machine

parameters.name: relay_drop_out_volts_nominal
parameters.provenance: CHOSEN to satisfy BH-06's 'great difference between the pull-in and drop-out voltages'. Ratio 2.5/6.5 = 0.38, a wide hysteresis by relay standards, which is what SDC claims to have deliberately engineered.
parameters.per_relay_spread: +/- 0.4 V, correlated with that relay's pull-in spread

parameters.name: closed_contact_resistance_ohm
parameters.provenance: CHOSEN, nominal. MM says the rotary switch uses silver-plated circuits and beryllium-copper fingers 'to provide low contact resistance'. Small but non-zero keeps the conductance matrix well-conditioned.

parameters.name: circuit_breaker_trip_current_amps
parameters.provenance: EL-02 gives 1.5 A continuous as the supply RATING; EL-12 verifies the breaker is in the total return and that SDC expects programming shorts to trip it. Equating the rating to the trip point is inference. It is a thermal breaker, so it needs a time-current curve, not an instantaneous threshold.
parameters.recommended_model: trip when the time-integral of (I - I_trip) over a sliding window exceeds a threshold; instantaneous trip above roughly 3x. A dead + to - short draws V_oc/R_src = 19.4 A on this profile and must trip immediately.

parameters.name: relay_actuation_time_ms
parameters.provenance: CHOSEN. Required to exist by BH-12 (carry propagation, 'push slowly', 'not designed for high-speed operation'), unconstrained in value by any source.

CORRECTION-01.target: find-relays.json, the proposed indicator-lamp series operating resistance of about 40 ohm, and REC-07 which advises making the lamp resistance LOWER at the series operating point so the coil can pull in.
CORRECTION-01.finding: The direction of REC-07 is right (a tungsten lamp running cooler in series does drop its resistance below its full-rail hot value) but the MAGNITUDE proposed silently breaks the model. With R_lamp = 40 and R_coil = 185, the divider ratio is 185/225.7 = 0.82, so the coil sees 10.66 V through the lamp against a proposed 7.5 V pull-in - a margin of 3.16 V, or 42%. Bypassing the lamp then buys only 2.3 V on a relay that already had 3.16 V of headroom. Under the full six-relay load the rail sags only ~0.87 V and the coil still sees ~9.9 V, still 2.4 V clear of pull-in.
CORRECTION-01.consequence: Under those numbers the Book IV counter ALWAYS works, the errata bypass circuit is never needed, and BH-02 - the only relay failure SDC ever documented - is erased. This is precisely the failure mode the gap brief warned about.
CORRECTION-01.resolution: The lamp must be COMPARABLE TO OR LARGER THAN the coil in the series path, not a quarter of it. MV601-REF-A uses R_lamp 131 ohm against R_coil 150 ohm, a divider ratio of 0.53. This is also the only reading consistent with EL-09, where SDC calls the lamps genuine current limiters for the coils - a 40 ohm element beside a 185 ohm coil limits almost nothing and would not warrant the comparison.
CORRECTION-01.note: This does not impugn find-relays.json, which explicitly flagged all of its numbers as the author's own and unverified. It is the arithmetic check that file invited.

part_5_fidelity_contract.note: Executable acceptance tests. Each states the circuit, the expected computed value under MV601-REF-A, and the primary citation for the behaviour being reproduced. A build that passes AT-01 through AT-06 has reproduced every electrically-observable behaviour SDC documented. Numbers below were computed, not estimated.

tests.name: Book I Experiment 9 canonical latch pulls in and holds THROUGH the lamp
tests.circuit: + -> pushbutton contacts -> 1C -> lamp -> 1E -> coil -> 1F -> -, lightly loaded machine (one relay, its own lamp, power lamp)
tests.assertion: V_coil 6.93 V > V_pullin 6.5 V, so the relay PULLS IN. Margin 0.43 V (6.6%). Hold path is the same path, and 6.93 V is far above V_dropout 2.5 V, so it HOLDS. PASS.
tests.sensitivity: This is the test that fails first if pull-in is raised. Raising V_pullin above ~6.9 V breaks the canonical latch and the simulator becomes unable to run Book I.

tests.name: Book IV three-bit counter is MARGINAL when driven via C
tests.circuit: six relays energised through their series lamps, plus the binary output lamps and the power lamp lit
tests.assertion: V_coil 6.67 V sits only 0.17 V above nominal V_pullin 6.5 V. With the verified per-relay spread of BH-08 modelled at +/- 0.7 V, roughly four of six relays have a pull-in above 6.67 V and FAIL. This reproduces SDC's exact wording: 'Relays which perform to satisfaction in every other case may not perform adequately in this circuit.' PASS.
tests.sensitivity: This is the test that fails first if pull-in is lowered or if the lamp is modelled as too small a resistance. Lowering V_pullin below ~6.2 V, or dropping R_lamp toward 40 ohm, makes the counter always work and erases the documented failure. See CORRECTION-01.

tests.name: The errata alternate counter is RELIABLE, and the lamp still lights
tests.circuit: coil driven E-to-F at full rail; C tied to the negative rail so the lamp hangs from E as a shunt
tests.assertion: V_coil 12.94 V is roughly twice V_pullin even at the top of the per-relay spread, so every relay pulls in reliably. The shunt lamp still carries current and still glows. PASS. Together AT-02 and AT-03 reproduce the failure AND the published fix - the pair is the real acceptance criterion, and neither test is meaningful alone.

tests.name: A common 1961 resistor value lands the coil inside the hysteresis band
tests.circuit: + -> R_bias -> 1E -> coil -> 1F -> - (no lamp in path; the Book VII bias circuit enters at E)
tests.assertion: Band is (V_dropout 2.5, V_pullin 6.5). Standard E12 5% values 180, 220, 270, 330, 390 and 470 ohm ALL land strictly inside it. 150 ohm sits exactly at pull-in, which is where the descending search of BH-09 terminates; 120 ohm and below pull the relay in at power-on and fail step 1; 560 and 680 ohm approach drop-out. PASS.
tests.bonus: The profile also reproduces BH-10 without being asked to: several adjacent values are simultaneously valid, exactly as SDC warns. And it predicts the Book VII kit's useful range - roughly 100 ohm to 700 ohm - which is a falsifiable prediction if a kit ever surfaces. See OQ-01.

tests.name: Six coils plus lamps stay under the published 1.5 A
tests.circuit: worst realistic published case: six relays energised via C (0.277 A total), plus six binary output lamps and the power lamp across the rail (0.566 A total)
tests.assertion: 0.844 A against a 1.5 A rating. The breaker does NOT trip during any ordinary published program, and the 44% headroom matches MM's claim that the parts are 'conservatively designed'. PASS.
tests.adversarial_check: Driving all six coils directly at E (0.518 A) while lighting all thirteen lamps across the rail (1.05 A) reaches 1.57 A and DOES trip. So the breaker is reachable by an unusual program but not by a normal one, which is the correct qualitative behaviour per ERR p.1.

tests.name: A dead short trips the breaker immediately
tests.circuit: a single patch wire from + to -
tests.assertion: V_oc/R_src = 13.0/0.67 = 19.4 A, about 13x the trip current. Instantaneous trip. Reproduces ERR p.1: 'If a programming error has caused a short circuit, push the circuit breaker after correcting the error.' PASS.

tests.name: The C/E distinction is observable on the very first relay lesson
tests.assertion: With 1X/1E the relay operates and its lamp stays DARK. Swapping to 1X/1C, the relay operates and its lamp LIGHTS. Both must energise the relay; only the lamp differs. PASS trivially under a network solve; impossible to get right by accident under a boolean core.

tests.name: Lamp across C-E alone lights without operating the relay
tests.citation: derived from BH-01; NOT demonstrated in any manual
tests.assertion: Powering 1C and 1E with 1F unconnected lights the lamp and leaves the relay off. This is a consequence of the verified topology but is NOT a reproduction of any published behaviour, so it is a regression guard, not evidence. Tagged [unverified] as a behavioural claim.

part_6_invariants.note: The single most useful result of this gap. The profile is five absolute numbers, but only THREE DIMENSIONLESS RATIOS are actually load-bearing. Tune these; the absolute ohms follow from the current budget alone.

invariants.name: lamp divider ratio
invariants.meaning: the fraction of rail voltage a coil receives when driven through its own indicator lamp
invariants.constraint: alpha must be LOW enough that bypassing the lamp is a meaningful intervention (BH-02) and HIGH enough that the canonical latch still works (BH-04). Roughly 0.45 to 0.60. The prior proposal's 0.82 is out of range and breaks BH-02.

invariants.name: normalised pull-in
invariants.meaning: pull-in as a fraction of the unloaded rail
invariants.constraint: beta must sit JUST BELOW alpha. That single relation is what simultaneously makes the canonical latch work and the loaded counter fail, because rail sag under load is what pushes alpha*V_rail below V_pullin. If beta > alpha, Book I breaks. If beta << alpha, the errata is erased. The whole gap reduces to this inequality: beta slightly less than alpha.

invariants.name: normalised drop-out
invariants.meaning: drop-out as a fraction of the unloaded rail
invariants.constraint: gamma must be well below beta to satisfy BH-06's 'great difference', and low enough that AT-04's E12 sweep has several values inside (gamma*V, beta*V).

part_6_invariants.headline: The correct summary of this gap is not 'we need five numbers'. It is: pull-in must sit just below the lamp-divided rail voltage, and rail sag under load must be able to push it across. Everything else is scale.

per_event_procedure: 1. Build the node set: union-find over patch wires and currently-closed contacts. Elements (coils, lamps, resistors, capacitors, source, motor) are never collapsed.
2. Stamp a conductance matrix G and current vector i. Ground the - node. Stamp the source as a Thevenin pair (V_oc, R_src) between + and -.
3. Solve G v = i by dense LU. The matrix is on the order of 60x60; this is microseconds and needs no sparse machinery.
4. INNER FIXED POINT for lamp nonlinearity: recompute each R_lamp from its own current and re-solve. Converges in 3 to 5 passes; the exponent 0.36 is gentle. Damp if it oscillates.

5. Evaluate relays with HYSTERESIS: V_coil >= that relay's pull_in -> energise; V_coil <= that relay's drop_out -> de-energise; otherwise HOLD PREVIOUS STATE. The hold branch is what makes Book VII expressible and what makes the state update well-defined.
6. OUTER FIXED POINT: if any relay changed state, the contact set changed, so go to step 1. Cap the iterations.

7. If the outer loop does not converge within the cap, that is NOT an error. It is a real oscillator - a relay buzzer, which Book VII builds deliberately. Report it as oscillation and drive the display from a time-averaged state.

degenerate_cases.case: a node with no conductive path to the source
degenerate_cases.handling: floating. Do not solve it; mark it unpowered. Do not assume 0 V, and never treat 'floating' as 'grounded'.

degenerate_cases.case: a coil sitting inside the hysteresis band at power-on with no prior state
degenerate_cases.handling: power-on state is OFF. This matters: ERR p.3 twice instructs users to turn power off and on again to reset a game, which only makes sense if power-on is a defined reset.

every transfer contact (relay, pushbutton, slide switch, rotary wiper) must have a genuine both-open interval. Carried forward from find-relays.json REC-04, where SDC states the feature 'is necessary for the proper operation of some MINIVAC circuits'.
open the entire negative return (EL-12), so ALL rails die at once, not just the offending branch. Requires an explicit user reset, matching the physical push-button breaker.

part_7_algorithm.book7_transient_note: Capacitors need real time-stepping against the coil and any series resistor. Gate this behind a flag. Books I-VI contain no reactive element and need only the DC solve. NOTE for whoever implements it: because there is no filter capacitor (EL-10), a Book VII capacitor connected across the rails charges toward the PEAK, not the average - about 20 V rather than 13 V on this profile - which materially changes the kick energy. See OQ-03.

part_8_book7_scope_ruling.question: CAP-09 offers an exit: descope Book VII, and bias resistors, capacitors and hysteresis go with it. Does that let the core fall back to boolean?
part_8_book7_scope_ruling.answer: NO. Descoping Book VII removes capacitors and the bias-resistor TECHNIQUE, but it does not remove the resistive solver, and it does not remove hysteresis.
reasoning: AT-01, AT-02, AT-03, AT-05, AT-06 and AT-07 are ALL Books I-IV plus the errata. They stand entirely without Book VII and they all require a network solve.

Hysteresis specifically survives the descope. Even with no bias resistors, a coil whose drive voltage varies with machine load (BH-02) needs distinct pull-in and drop-out thresholds, or it chatters at the boundary in circuits where it demonstrably does not chatter on real hardware.

What descoping Book VII DOES buy: no transient integration, no capacitor element, no per-relay bias resistance table, and no need to resolve OQ-01 or OQ-03. That is a real saving in the time-domain machinery, and it is the right first milestone.
part_8_book7_scope_ruling.recommendation: Build the DC resistive core now with hysteresis. Ship Books I-VI on it. Add the transient path for Book VII later behind a flag. The core does not change when Book VII arrives; only the element set grows.

open_questions.question: What resistor values shipped in the Book VII kit?
open_questions.status: NOT SETTLED BY THE SOURCES. Book VII says only 'the highest valued resistor in the kit' (BH-09) and prints one worked example at 22 ohm (EL-07) plus a motor-slowing note naming 15, 22, 33 ohm (EL-08). No parts list appears anywhere. MV601-REF-A PREDICTS the useful bias range is about 100 to 700 ohm, which is falsifiable.
open_questions.what_would_settle_it: A photograph or scan of the Book VII kit contents or its parts list, or a Book VII page I did not render (PDF pp.2-10 and 16-55 have no usable OCR text layer and were not all imaged).

open_questions.question: What are the actual relay and lamp part numbers?
open_questions.status: NOT SETTLED. MM gives spare part 6437 'Relay' at $6.00 and 6435 'Light Assembly' at $1.00 and no specification for either. Three web searches found no measured value or part number anywhere on the open web. The only under-chassis evidence would be a photograph, and all four local photographs are top-down panel shots.
open_questions.what_would_settle_it: An under-chassis photograph of a surviving unit at sufficient resolution to read the relay's stamped part number and the lamp's base type, then a 1961 datasheet. Failing that, a multimeter on a surviving unit: coil resistance cold, lamp resistance cold, and a variable-supply sweep for pull-in and drop-out on each of the six relays. That single measurement session would close this gap outright and replace all of part 4.

open_questions.question: Does 120 Hz ripple on the unfiltered rails (EL-10) matter?
open_questions.status: NOT SETTLED, but I recommend modelling the rail as its DC AVERAGE at v1 and I can justify it. A relay coil's own inductance (order 1 to 3 H against 150 ohm gives L/R of 7 to 20 ms) is comparable to or longer than the 8.3 ms half-period, so coil CURRENT is substantially self-smoothed and the armature responds to the average. The lamp filament's thermal mass smooths the light similarly. Two second-order effects to note: lamp resistance is set by RMS rather than average current (form factor 1.11 for a rectified sine), and Book VII capacitors charge toward the peak, not the average.
open_questions.what_would_settle_it: An oscilloscope trace across + and - on a surviving unit under load, and a coil inductance measurement.

open_questions.question: Is 'nominal 12 volts output' really the loaded figure at 1.5 A?
open_questions.status: NOT SETTLED. R_src = 0.67 ohm depends entirely on this reading. If 12 V is instead a marketing round-down of the 13 V unloaded figure, the true source impedance is unknown and could be much lower, which would weaken AT-02's rail-sag mechanism and require pull-in to be re-tuned upward toward alpha.
open_questions.what_would_settle_it: A loaded-rail measurement on a surviving unit, or any SDC advertising or dealer literature quoting a load regulation figure.

open_questions.question: Relay actuation and release times.
open_questions.status: NOT SETTLED. BH-12 proves they are observable and load-bearing (SDC tells users to push slowly and to hold long enough for carry propagation) but no source gives a number. 12 ms / 8 ms are placeholders.

open_questions.question: Is the per-relay pull-in spread really as wide as +/- 0.7 V?
open_questions.status: NOT SETTLED in magnitude, though its EXISTENCE is verified by BH-08 (SDC demands per-relay characterisation) and BH-02 ('relays which perform to satisfaction in every other case'). The +/- 0.7 V figure is chosen to make roughly four of six relays fail AT-02, which is a guess at what 'somewhat strained' meant in practice.

known_discrepancy_carried_forward.note: Recording, not resolving, per the project rule. Both addresses are primary and both appear in the sources I read for THIS gap.
known_discrepancy_carried_forward.watertown: The Maintenance Manual cover, the Maintenance Manual spare-parts order block ('Watertown 72, Massachusetts'), the errata sheet header and footer, and the Book VII back cover ALL read 'Scientific Development Corporation, 372 Main Street, Watertown, Massachusetts'.
known_discrepancy_carried_forward.cambridge: The panel legend in prebrief/images/image_3.jpg reads 'Scientific Development Corporation, Cambridge, Massachusetts' (not re-verified by me in this gap; carried from prior findings).
known_discrepancy_carried_forward.ruling: Do not pick one. Both are primary artifacts of the same company at different times or in different media.

part_10_what_would_overturn_this: A measurement session on a surviving unit. Coil resistance, lamp resistance cold and at the series operating point, and a pull-in/drop-out sweep on all six relays would replace part 4 wholesale and demote MV601-REF-A to a historical note. This is the single highest-value action available and it is not a research action.
A Book VII kit parts list showing resistor values outside roughly 100-700 ohm would falsify the AT-04 prediction and force R_coil to move.

Any SDC document giving a lamp part number. If the lamp turns out to be a low-resistance type (say under 60 ohm at the series point), CORRECTION-01 is wrong, alpha rises above 0.8, and the whole profile must be rebuilt around a much higher pull-in near 10.5 V - a machine with almost no design margin, which I judge unlikely but cannot exclude.
Evidence that the supply DOES contain a filter capacitor omitted from the troubleshooting schematic. That would not change the DC solve but would invalidate EL-11 and OQ-03's peak-charging note.
